Recipient and theme lengths are paired [random variables](why-random-variables.qmd) on each dative token. Their **covariance** is the [expected value](expected-values.qmd) of the product of their centered deviations, so its sign records whether those paired deviations tend to point in the same direction.

The earlier [vector and matrix
primer](variance-and-covariance.qmd#vectors-matrices-and-covariance) organizes
many variances and covariances in one covariance matrix. This page focuses on
one off-diagonal entry and the paired observations that determine it.

The [dative data discussion](poisson-distribution.qmd#the-dative-data) defines one row
as one corpus token and the two lengths as word counts. The first verified row
pairs a one-word recipient with a 14-word theme; covariance uses that pairing,
not two independently sampled marginal values.

We define covariance as an expectation over paired deviations, compute its empirical and sample forms, and then keep the denominator and measurement units visible in their interpretation.

## Definition

For random variables $R$ and $T$,

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(R,T)
=\mathbb{E}\left[(R-\mathbb{E}[R])(T-\mathbb{E}[T])\right].
$$

Expanding the product gives the equivalent identity

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(R,T)
=\mathbb{E}[RT]-\mathbb{E}[R]\mathbb{E}[T].
$$

More explicitly,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[(R-\mathbb{E}[R])(T-\mathbb{E}[T])]
&=\mathbb{E}[RT]
-\mathbb{E}[R]\mathbb{E}[T]\\
&\quad-\mathbb{E}[T]\mathbb{E}[R]
+\mathbb{E}[R]\mathbb{E}[T]\\
&=\mathbb{E}[RT]-\mathbb{E}[R]\mathbb{E}[T].
\end{aligned}
$$

For constants $a,b,c,d$,

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(aR+b,cT+d)
=ac\,\operatorname{Cov}(R,T).
$$

Covariance has units equal to the product of the two measurement units. Here both lengths are measured in words, so covariance is measured in words squared.

## Empirical covariance of dative lengths

```{r}
#| label: dative-covariance
library(ggplot2)

dative <- read.csv(
  "data/english-dative/dative-alternation.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  na.strings = c("", "NA")
)
R <- dative$recipient_length_words
T <- dative$theme_length_words
mean_R <- mean(R)
mean_T <- mean(T)
covariance_population <- mean((R - mean_R) * (T - mean_T))
covariance_identity <- mean(R * T) - mean_R * mean_T

joint <- as.data.frame(table(recipient = R, theme = T), responseName = "count")
joint$recipient <- as.integer(as.character(joint$recipient))
joint$theme <- as.integer(as.character(joint$theme))
joint <- subset(joint, count > 0)

stopifnot(
  length(R) == 3263L,
  abs(covariance_population - covariance_identity) < 1e-12,
  abs(cov(R, T) * (length(R) - 1) / length(R) -
        covariance_population) < 1e-12
)

data.frame(mean_R, mean_T, covariance_population,
           sample_covariance = cov(R, T))
```

The empirical population covariance is `r sprintf("%.3f", covariance_population)` words squared. Its positive sign means that same-direction deviations make a slightly larger average contribution than opposite-direction deviations.

The quadrant contributions make that small remainder visible. Relative to the
two empirical means, 383 high–high rows contribute 2,889.48 centered-product
units and 1,595 low–low rows contribute 2,842.40. The 633 low-recipient,
high-theme rows contribute $-2{,}327.02$, while the 652 high-recipient,
low-theme rows contribute $-2{,}478.02$. Dividing the net sum by 3,263 yields
the reported covariance. Large positive and negative contributions mostly
cancel.

```{r}
#| label: plot-dative-covariance
#| fig-cap: "Observed dative length pairs. Point area shows token count; accent lines mark the two empirical means."
ggplot(joint, aes(theme, recipient, size = count)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey35", alpha = 0.65) + # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean_T, color = "#8B1A1A", linewidth = 0.65) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean_R, color = "#8B1A1A", linewidth = 0.65) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 7) +
  labs(x = "Theme length (words)", y = "Recipient length (words)",
       size = "Token count") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The cloud extends far on both axes but has little diagonal organization. Covariance alone does not show nonlinear dependence, and its magnitude cannot be compared across variables with different units or scales.

## Sample covariance

When rows are treated as a sample for estimating a population covariance, the
familiar [estimator](../statistical-inference/properties-of-estimators.qmd)—a
rule mapping the random sample to an estimate of the population covariance—is

$$
s_{R,T}
=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(R_i-\overline R)(T_i-\overline T).
$$

The page reports the empirical population covariance of the prepared dative table because its immediate target is that table's joint distribution. Later inferential work must state a sampling unit and accommodate repeated verbs and speakers.

R's `cov(R, T)` uses the $n-1$ estimator. Multiplying it by $(n-1)/n$ produces
the $1/n$ empirical-population covariance displayed here, which is exactly the
conversion checked in code.

## Check your understanding

1. Verify covariance with the $\mathbb{E}[RT]-\mathbb{E}[R]\mathbb{E}[T]$ identity.
2. Identify which quadrants around the mean lines contribute positively.
3. Explain the difference between the two denominators used above.
4. Why can a covariance near zero coexist with dependence?
5. A student computes covariance after separately shuffling recipient and theme
   lengths. Which information required by covariance has been destroyed?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. $\mathbb{E}[RT]-\mathbb{E}[R]\mathbb{E}[T]=0.284045$ words squared, matching the mean centered product. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Observations above both means and observations below both means contribute positively because the two centered factors have the same sign. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Dividing by $n$ treats the represented rows as the empirical population, whereas dividing by $n-1$ applies the usual sample-covariance degrees-of-freedom correction. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Covariance can be near zero under strong nonlinear or sign-canceling dependence, because it summarizes only average linear co-movement. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
5. Shuffling destroys the within-token pairings that determine each centered
   product, even though both marginal distributions remain unchanged.

</details>

Covariance averages paired centered products, so contributions from same-sign
and opposite-sign quadrants may largely cancel. The choice between $n$ and
$n-1$ in the denominator depends on whether the target is an empirical
population quantity or an estimator. The [correlation page](correlation.qmd)
standardizes covariance to remove its units.
